prompt_text:
The figure summarizes how ferroptosis is controlled at the plasma membrane by balancing lipid peroxidation against several protective systems. Its central message is that ferroptosis results from iron-driven oxidation of phospholipids, especially PUFA-containing membrane lipids, and can be suppressed through multiple parallel antioxidant pathways.

One major route is the cystine–GSH–GPX4 axis: cystine import through system x_c^- supports glutathione production, which GPX4 uses to reduce phospholipid hydroperoxides to less harmful alcohols. The figure also shows the FSP1–CoQ/vitamin K pathway, where FSP1 uses NAD(P)H to regenerate reduced CoQ or vitamin K forms that trap lipid radicals in membranes. A third protective branch involves cholesterol synthesis intermediates, including squalene and 7-DHC, which appear to limit lipid peroxidation. The GCH1–BH4 pathway is shown as another radical-scavenging system, with vitamin E and related lipophilic antioxidants also blocking damaging lipid radicals.

The lower part illustrates the chemistry of phospholipid peroxidation: initiation, propagation, and termination of lipid radicals ultimately cause membrane rupture. A comparison of phospholipid composition highlights that PUFA incorporation promotes ferroptosis, whereas MUFA-rich phospholipids are anti-ferroptotic. Several inhibitors are marked, including erastin, BSO, RSL3, and ML210, which target these defense pathways.
